cta.body: No queue, no invite, no reservation list. Whoever asks first, gets it.
cta.title: Pick a name while it's still unclaimed

different.c1_body: There is no waitlist, no queue, no referral ladder and no reserved block of premium names held back for insiders. The registry starts empty. Every unregistered name is available to whoever asks for it first, and "first" is decided by block height and position — not by us.
different.c2_body: There is no expiry date in the protocol, no annual fee and no check-in window you can miss. Registration is once. A name leaves your control only when you sign a command transferring or selling it — there is no mechanism, for us or anyone, to reclaim it.
different.c3_body: A name is bound to your Ed25519 public key, and every change is a command you sign yourself. We never hold your keys and never move a name on your behalf. Nothing in the system can be operated by us that you did not authorise.
different.c4_body: List a name for sale at your price, unlist it, or buy one that's listed. Sale proceeds credit your balance net of a flat 5% service fee, and a bid that loses a race is returned to your balance rather than lost. Ownership changes hands as a signed, on-chain command like everything else.
different.c5_body: .kerrigan, .krgn, .private, .secure and .safe. Same protocol, same pricing, same guarantees — pick the one that reads best for you.
different.c6_body: Change the address behind your name whenever you rotate wallets. Everyone who knows the name keeps paying the right place, and nobody has to be told. The old address simply stops being the answer.
different.title: Open from day one

faq.a1: A record in the registry binding your name to your public key and a target address. Only a command signed by that key can change it. Because the record's whole history is on-chain and the viewing key is public, your claim to it is something a third party can verify without asking us.
faq.a2: The command history is in the Kerrigan blockchain and the software that interprets it is open source, so the registry can be reconstructed by anyone with a Kerrigan node and the published viewing key. Resolution can continue without us. That is the reason the design puts the commands on-chain rather than in a database we control.
faq.a3: Commands travel as shielded transactions, so amounts and addresses stay off the public ledger. A name is a way for someone to reach you, not a window into your balance or your history — closer to publishing an email address than a bank statement.
faq.a4: Labels are restricted to lowercase a–z, digits and hyphens, so the homograph tricks that plague Unicode identifiers aren't possible here. A name can still be similar to another — but it's short enough to read in full, which is not true of the address it replaces.
faq.a5: Run an indexer node. It scans Kerrigan with the published viewing key, replays every command, computes the state root independently and compares it against the root anchored on-chain. The documentation has the address, the key and a one-command Docker image.
faq.a6: It is rejected rather than applied — an invalid command can never corrupt the registry, which is what the on-chain proof enforces. Where the payment can be attributed to you, it is returned to your balance; where the command is malformed past the point of identifying a payer, it cannot be. The app validates commands before you send one.

roadmap.title: Where this goes from here
roadmap.lede: The protocol is finished in the sense that matters — names work, and the registry can be verified by anyone. What follows is about making them easier to use.
roadmap.r1_body: A block explorer shows you transactions. This one will show you names: every registration, every address change, every transfer of ownership, every listing and sale — laid out as one searchable history you can follow without running a node yourself.
roadmap.r2_title: Built into the wallets you already use
roadmap.r2_body: The point of a name is that you never touch the address. That is only fully true once your wallet resolves names itself, so it is where the effort goes next. If you build a Kerrigan wallet, we would rather do this with you than around you.
roadmap.r3_title: Shaped by what you ask for
roadmap.r3_body: Past those two, the roadmap is deliberately unwritten. Tell us what is missing, what gets in your way, or what you expected to find and did not — that is what decides the order of everything after this.

trust.callout_body: The property is fraud-evident, not fraud-preventing. A bad batch can reach the chain and be contradicted afterwards; nothing here can stop it being published in the first place. What the design guarantees is that it cannot be hidden — and that you never needed our cooperation to find out.
trust.callout_title: Being honest about what this is
trust.lede: Most name services ask you to believe a database. This one is designed so that believing is unnecessary: every command that ever changed the registry is a shielded Kerrigan transaction, and the key needed to read them is published.
trust.s1_body: Registering, updating, listing or buying a name is a shielded note sent to the protocol address. The amount is the payment and the encrypted memo is the signed command, in one transaction — so intent and payment can't be separated, reordered or invented after the fact.
trust.s2_body: The registrar publishes the protocol address and its viewing key. Anyone can scan the chain with it and recover every command ever issued, from genesis, in the exact order the blockchain fixed.
trust.s3_body: Feed that stream through the open-source indexer and you derive the registry state yourself, independently. Run it in one command with the published Docker image, or read the source and build your own.
trust.s4_body: The state root is anchored on-chain with a zero-knowledge proof that the transition rules were followed. If the operator ever censored a paid command, invented a transfer or reordered history, every independent indexer computes a different root and contradicts it — without permission or special access.
trust.title: You don't have to trust us. You can check.
